newsitem.title: NICARAGUA: Bad roads threaten Nicaraguan coffee harvest.
newsitem.headline: Bad roads threaten Nicaraguan coffee harvest.

text.p: The chief of Nicaragua's coffee growers association said on Tuesday that more than 80 percent of the 1996-97 coffee harvest was at risk because of bad roads, which have been made worse by recent torrential rains.

David Robleto, president of the Nicaraguan Union of Coffee Growers (Unicafe), said of the 1,215,867 quintales (100-pound bags) that Nicaragua expects to produce in 1996-97, some 987,727 could be affected by the poor state of the roads.

Robleto also confirmed that he has accepted the post of Minister of Foreign Cooperation under President-elect Arnoldo Aleman, who will take office January 10. Robleto and Aleman are neighbors in the coffee-growing hills of western Managua.

Recent torrential rains, and the failure to repair roads destroyed by Hurricane Cesar in July, have left 587 miles (947 kms) of roads in coffee-growing regions damaged, Robleto told a news conference.
"It's clearly understood that if the most affected roads are not repaired, we are not going to meet our production goal," he said.
The state of the roads has raised transportation costs by 10 percent, he said.
Robleto said he met with the Transportation Minister Pablo Vijil on Monday and was told money was short but that there was enough to repair roads that were currently unpassable.
Robleto said he will meet with ministry officials on Wednesday to determine which roads will be given top priority.
Nicaragua plans to export 1,033,487 quintales of coffee in 1996-97 worth an estimated $112.65 million, down from the 1,158,742 quintales it exported in 1995-96.
Robleto said that as of November 20, some 85,000 quintales of Nicaraguan coffee had been harvested, and that the heavy rains would delay this year's harvest.
The coffee disease "la roya" is affecting the departments (provinces) of Jinotega, Matagalpa, Nueva Segovia and the Pacific plateau region, he said.
"The effects of the roya will be seen in the 1997-98 harvest," Robleto said.

Robleto said an outbreak of cholera in the department of Matagalpa that has sickened 770 people and killed 33 is affecting the availibility of labor. The Health Ministry is attending 177 farms in that region.

Regarding his replacement at the head of Unicafe, Robleto said an executive committee selected from within the organization will take over management of Unicafe until a new president is elected. Robleto said he will head the interim committee.
